solution_options.fusion_note: Both methods must look at the same small tissue area and their data must be aligned to a common time step, because alternating separate probes cannot guarantee the same spot and the acquisition rates differ. Start from one classification model per method with block scaling or per-method scores, keep a separate calibration and diagnostic check for each instrument, and validate the fused model on held-out samples or patients. The fused model must beat the better single method, otherwise the second instrument is not justified.

citations.quote: It is crucial that the spectral information obtained by different methods-Mid-IR, NIR, Raman, and fluorescence spectra-is collected from the same small, even pinpoint, area of the sample.
Ultimately, the measurement data must be normalized to a common time step.
Variables obtained from different spectral methods are not equivalent.
One of the challenges of multispectral analysis is the need to simultaneously connect at least two independently operating measuring instruments.

chemometrics_note: Tissue classification needs calibration or classification models (for example PCA or PLS-DA) built on labelled samples and validated on held-out samples or patients; a model is specific to the tissue matrix and tumour type and must be rebuilt when either changes.
realtime_tracking_note: Real-time use needs fast acquisition and a fiber link that keeps the spectrometer away from the measurement point; if two methods are combined, their different acquisition rates must be aligned to a common time step.
future_direction: If the bench work identifies the most informative spectral regions, a compact multisensor or LED-based sensor could be a later development step, following the described sequence of lab trials, then a chemometric model or a customised system.

proposal.what_would_change_it: If the tissue fluoresces strongly at the Raman excitation, or if the MIR fiber link from the measurement point cannot be realised, the balance shifts toward Raman or toward the combined MIR-ATR + Raman option; the team's go/no-go numbers would also change the choice.
proposal.next_step: Run the bench feasibility test on representative tumour and healthy tissue samples against histology before any patient use is considered.

brief_answer: Nothing supplied covers regulatory approval or clinical readiness, so starting on patients next month is not supported by this material. Technically, the sources give the strongest tissue-classification precedent for MIR-ATR, with Raman (the team's proposal) also worth testing and a combined MIR-ATR + Raman option as a later hypothesis. Next step: a bench feasibility test on representative tumour and healthy tissue against histology, with go/no-go numbers agreed with the team.
